title: An Unprotected Wetland of International Importance in the Central Asian Flyway: Waterbird Assemblages Reveal the Global Conservation Value of Perungulam, Tamil Nadu, Southeast India
content:
The graphical abstract summarizes the first systematic surveys at Perungulam wetland in southeast India (2021–2024). The study recorded 69 waterbird species, including resident breeders (21 species), resident nonbreeders (19 species), and winter migrants (29 species), with annual abundances consistently exceeding 30,000 individuals across all years. The wetland meets Ramsar Criteria 2, 4, 5, and 6 by supporting threatened species, breeding populations, large congregations, and multiple species that exceed the 1% biogeographical population threshold. These establish Perungulam as a site of international importance within the Central Asian Flyway and as a priority consideration for designation as a community reserve or Ramsar site for habitat protection.


ABSTRACT

Wetlands in India remain poorly documented despite their significance in sustaining migratory and resident waterbirds within the Central Asian Flyway (CAF). This pivotal systematic assessment of the waterbird assemblage of Perungulam wetland, Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, southeast India, is based on surveys conducted from June 2021 to May 2024. Direct and block count methods were employed to document species composition and abundance. Species were assessed against global conservation and population status, South Asian biogeographical population (BGP) estimates, and Ramsar Convention criteria for wetlands of international importance. A total of 69 waterbird species were recorded, including 21 resident breeders, 19 resident nonbreeders, and 29 winter visitors. Waterbird community structure was highly uneven, with eight species accounting for 75% of the total abundance. Species richness increased from 58 to 65 species across 3 years. Although most species were classified as Least Concern, the wetland consistently supported one globally Vulnerable species (Curlew Sandpiper), moderately supporting Ramsar Criterion 2, and four additional near-threatened species (Black-tailed Godwit, Bar-tailed Godwit, Spot-billed Pelican, and Asian Woollyneck) of conservation concern. We recorded breeding of 21 waterbird species, adding strong evidence to Ramsar Criterion 4. Repeated fortnightly surveys consistently recorded waterbird assemblages exceeding the Ramsar Criterion 5 threshold of 20,000 individuals, with cumulative counts ranging from 30,626 to 36,167 birds. Ramsar Criterion 6 assessment had strong evidence, with at least 10 species regularly exceeding their 1% BGP thresholds. Notably, Spot-billed Pelican (594–651 individuals vs. 100 threshold), Glossy Ibis (6510–7845 vs. 3000), Painted Stork (1270–1980 vs. 250), Little Cormorant, and Indian Spot-billed Duck consistently surpassed their respective thresholds. These findings support the level of evidence that Perungulam qualifies as a “Wetland of International Importance.” Immediate steps toward designation as a Community Reserve are strongly recommended, along with longer-term consideration of Ramsar listing to safeguard this critical wetland within the CAF.
